also: for (for those times, for a child)

terms.grammar: the comparative of an adjective or adverb without a second term
evidence: Cic. Sen. 55: senectūs est nātūrā loquācior (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin says “relatively long” with the comparative alone, which then means “rather, fairly, more than usual”: loquācior, rather talkative.

terms.gloss: for, considering, relative to (the times, the person)
terms.grammar: conjunction: ut with in + ablative, or with a clause, restricting what is said
evidence: Cic. Brut. 102: scrīptor, ut temporibus illīs, lūculentus (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Sen. 12: multae, ut in homine Rōmānō, litterae (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Fam. 12.2.2: nōnnihil, ut in tantīs malīs, est prōfectum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The Latin for “good for those times”, “learned, for a Roman”: ut limits the praise to the circumstances (Lewis & Short, s.v. ut: “for, as, considering”).

evidence: Liv. 21.29: atrōcius quam prō numerō pugnantium (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Sen. 27: agere prō vīribus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Measures a thing against a standard: prō vīribus, as far as one’s strength allows; atrōcius quam prō numerō, fiercer than the numbers would suggest (Lewis & Short).

phrases.english: old age is by nature rather talkative

phrases.latin: Caelius Antipater, scrīptor, ut temporibus illīs, lūculentus
phrases.english: Caelius Antipater, a fine writer for those times

phrases.latin: multae, ut in homine Rōmānō, litterae
